newsitem.title: CANADA: Alberta loosens ties to government-owned bank.
newsitem.headline: Alberta loosens ties to government-owned bank.

text.p: The Alberta government on Tuesday introduced changes to legislation governing Alberta Treasury Branches, aimed at forging an arm's length relationship between the government and the provincially owned bank.
But the Western Canadian province said the overhaul was not a precursor to a privatization of ATB and there were no plans to put the institution up for sale any time soon.
"With this legislation, ATB will operate with the same kinds of rules that other banks and financial institutions follow," Alberta Treasurer Stockwell Day said in a statement.

Alberta said the changes to the Alberta Treasury Branches Act were intended to provide clear powers for the institution's board and chief executive, replacing those previously held by the provincial treasurer.

Under the amendments, ATB's business would be restricted to providing services similar to other financial institutions, so depositors' money was not placed at risk in unrelated businesses, the government said.
That would prohibit it from acting as a receiver or liquidator, guaranteed unfixed sums of money or acting as an insurer.
It would also be required to establish "prudent loan and investment standards" and review its investment practices annually, Alberta said.

ATB and the Alberta government have come under public scrutiny over loans, often criticized as politically driven, to such figures as controversial sports entrepreneurs Peter Pocklington and Larry Ryckman as well as West Edmonton Mall developers, the Ghermezian family.
Also as part of the changes, ATB would be allowed to invest in such entities as trust companies, securities dealers and insurance companies, the government said.
But the provincial treasurer would still have the right to order ATB to stop any action he believed to be contrary to the act, which must be reviewed every five years, Alberta said.
